title.en: Section 1 - Conversation at a Travel Agency
title.zh: 第一部分 - 旅行社对话

sections.passage: A conversation between a customer and a travel agent. The customer, Mrs. Patterson, visits a travel agency to book a holiday package for her family. The travel agent, Tom, greets her and asks about her preferences. Mrs. Patterson explains that she wants to take her two children, aged 8 and 12, on a beach holiday somewhere warm. Tom suggests several destinations including Spain, Greece, and Turkey. Mrs. Patterson mentions that she has been to Spain before and would like to try somewhere new. Tom recommends a family resort in Crete, Greece, which has a children's club, a swimming pool, and is located near a sandy beach. The package includes flights from Heathrow Airport, airport transfers, and half-board accommodation at a four-star hotel. The total cost for the family would be 2,400 pounds for two weeks, departing on July 15th. Mrs. Patterson asks about travel insurance, and Tom explains that basic coverage is included but she can upgrade to comprehensive coverage for an additional 85 pounds per person. She also asks about excursions, and Tom mentions that there are optional trips to Knossos Palace and a boat trip to the island of Spinalonga, costing 45 and 35 pounds per adult respectively, with children paying half price. Mrs. Patterson decides to book the package with the insurance upgrade and both excursions.

title.en: Section 2 - Radio Programme about Local Events
title.zh: 第二部分 - 关于本地活动的广播节目

sections.passage: Welcome to Radio Millbrook's weekly community bulletin. I'm your host, Jenny Clarke, and today I'll be telling you about some exciting events happening in our area over the coming weeks. First up is the annual Millbrook Summer Fair, which will take place on Saturday the 28th of June in Victoria Park. The fair opens at 10 in the morning and runs until 6 in the evening. There will be stalls selling homemade cakes, preserves, and crafts, as well as a children's entertainer, a bouncy castle, and live music from the Millbrook Jazz Band. Entry is free, but donations to the local hospice are warmly welcomed. Next, I'm pleased to announce that the Millbrook Literary Festival is returning for its fifth year. It will be held from the 4th to the 7th of July at the Town Hall. This year's guest speakers include the bestselling crime novelist Sarah Blake and the travel writer and broadcaster Michael Chen. Ticket prices vary depending on the event, but a full festival pass costs just 30 pounds, which represents a saving of 40 percent compared to buying individual tickets. For younger residents, the Millbrook Youth Theatre is staging a production of Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream at the Community Arts Centre. Performances will run from the 10th to the 14th of July, with evening shows starting at 7:30 and a matinee on Saturday at 2:30. Tickets are 8 pounds for adults and 5 pounds for concessions. Finally, for those who enjoy outdoor activities, the Millbrook Walking Festival takes place over the weekend of the 20th and 21st of July. There are guided walks of varying difficulty, ranging from a gentle two-mile stroll along the riverside to a challenging twelve-mile hike across the moors. Participants should wear appropriate footwear and bring waterproof clothing, as the weather can be unpredictable. Registration is required in advance and can be done online at the council's website.

title.zh: 第三部分 - 两名学生之间的讨论

sections.passage: Two students, James and Priya, are discussing their upcoming group presentation for their Environmental Studies course. They need to present their research on renewable energy sources next Thursday. James has been researching solar power and has found some interesting statistics about the growth of solar panel installations in the UK over the past decade. He mentions that the cost of solar panels has dropped by approximately 80 percent since 2010, making it much more accessible for homeowners. Priya has been looking into wind energy and has gathered data showing that the UK is now the world's largest offshore wind energy producer. She has prepared several charts showing the capacity growth from 2015 to 2023. They discuss how to structure their presentation. James suggests starting with a brief overview of global energy consumption trends before moving into their specific topics. Priya agrees but thinks they should include a section on government policies that have promoted renewable energy adoption, such as feed-in tariffs and the Renewable Heat Incentive. They decide to divide the presentation into three main parts: the current energy landscape, the two renewable technologies they have researched, and policy recommendations for the future. James volunteers to create the introduction and the solar power section, while Priya will cover wind energy and the policy recommendations. They plan to meet on Tuesday evening to combine their sections and rehearse. Priya mentions that their professor, Dr. Williams, has emphasized the importance of using credible sources, so they agree to use only peer-reviewed journals and official government statistics. James asks about the presentation format, and Priya confirms that Dr. Williams requires PowerPoint slides with a maximum of fifteen slides and a speaking time of twenty minutes, followed by five minutes for questions from the audience.

title.en: Section 4 - University Lecture on Urban Planning
title.zh: 第四部分 - 关于城市规划的大学讲座

sections.passage: Good morning, everyone. Today's lecture is the third in our series on Urban Planning and Sustainable Development. In the previous two sessions, we examined the historical evolution of city design and the principles of sustainable architecture. Today, I want to focus on a concept that has gained significant traction in recent years: the fifteen-minute city. The fifteen-minute city is a urban planning model in which most daily necessities and services can be reached by means of walking or cycling within fifteen minutes from home. This concept was popularized by Professor Carlos Moreno of the Sorbonne University in Paris, and it has been adopted as a framework for urban development in cities around the world, including Melbourne, Barcelona, and most notably Paris, where Mayor Anne Hidalgo made it a central pillar of her 2020 re-election campaign. The fundamental idea is to reduce dependency on private cars by creating polycentric neighbourhoods where people can live, work, and access amenities locally. This approach has several documented benefits. First, it reduces carbon emissions by decreasing the need for long commutes. A study conducted in Paris found that implementing the fifteen-minute city model could reduce transportation-related emissions by up to 40 percent. Second, it promotes social cohesion by encouraging people to interact with their neighbours and local businesses. Third, it improves public health by encouraging active transportation such as walking and cycling. However, the concept is not without its critics. Some urban planners argue that it is primarily applicable to affluent neighbourhoods in developed cities, and that it could lead to increased gentrification and housing inequality. Critics also point out that not all types of employment can be localized — for example, factory workers, hospital staff, and emergency services personnel often need to travel to specific locations. Furthermore, implementing the fifteen-minute city model in existing cities requires substantial investment in infrastructure, including cycling lanes, pedestrian zones, and improved public transport networks. Despite these challenges, many cities are finding innovative ways to adopt elements of this model. For example, Barcelona has implemented its Superblocks programme, which restricts traffic in certain neighbourhood blocks and converts road space into green areas and community spaces. Milan similarly created pedestrian and cycling corridors during the COVID-19 pandemic, many of which have been made permanent. The key takeaway from today's lecture is that while the fifteen-minute city may not be universally applicable, its principles of accessibility, proximity, and sustainability offer valuable guidance for future urban planning initiatives.

title.zh: 文章1 - 巧克力的历史

sections.passage:
Chocolate is one of the most popular treats in the world, but its history stretches back thousands of years to the ancient civilizations of Central and South America. The story of chocolate begins with the cacao tree, Theobroma cacao, which is native to the tropical regions of the Amazon basin. The word Theobroma literally translates to 'food of the gods' in Greek, reflecting the reverence that ancient peoples held for this remarkable plant.

The earliest known use of cacao dates back to approximately 1900 BC, based on chemical analysis of ancient pottery vessels found in present-day Honduras. The Olmec civilization, which flourished in the Gulf Coast region of Mexico from around 1500 BC, is believed to have been the first to domesticate the cacao plant and prepare beverages from its beans. However, it was the Maya civilization that truly elevated cacao to a central role in their culture and society. The Maya prepared a frothy, bitter drink made from ground cacao seeds, water, cornmeal, chili peppers, and various spices. This beverage was consumed during religious ceremonies, used as currency in trade, and offered to the gods as a sacred tribute.

When the Aztec Empire rose to power in the 15th century, they adopted the Maya's reverence for cacao and incorporated it into their own culture. The Aztec emperor Montezuma II was reported to drink dozens of cups of a cacao-based beverage called xocolatl each day. Because cacao beans could not be grown in the dry highlands of central Mexico where the Aztec capital Tenochtitlan was located, they had to be obtained through trade or as tribute from conquered peoples, making cacao a luxury item accessible primarily to the elite.

European contact with chocolate began in 1502, when Christopher Columbus encountered a large canoe filled with cacao beans during his fourth voyage to the Americas. However, it was the Spanish conquistador Hernan Cortes who first recognized the commercial potential of cacao after observing its value among the Aztecs in the early 1520s. Cortes brought cacao beans back to Spain, where they were initially prepared as a bitter drink mixed with sugar and spices to suit European tastes. Over the following century, the consumption of chocolate spread throughout the European aristocracy, with chocolate houses opening in cities such as London, Paris, and Amsterdam.

The transformation of chocolate from an expensive beverage to an affordable solid treat occurred in the 19th century through several key innovations. In 1828, Dutch chemist Coenraad van Houten invented a hydraulic press that could extract cocoa butter from roasted cacao beans, leaving behind a dry cake that could be pulverized into cocoa powder. This process, known as Dutching, made chocolate drinks smoother and more palatable. In 1847, Joseph Fry of the British company J.S. Fry and Sons discovered that by mixing cocoa powder, sugar, and melted cocoa butter, he could create a paste that could be moulded into a solid bar — the first modern chocolate bar. Shortly after, in 1867, Swiss chocolatier Daniel Peter added condensed milk to chocolate, creating milk chocolate, a product he refined with the help of his neighbour Henri Nestle. These innovations democratized chocolate consumption and laid the foundation for the global chocolate industry we know today, which generates over 130 billion dollars in annual revenue.

title.en: Passage 2 - The Psychology of Decision Making

sections.passage:
Every day, the average adult makes approximately 35,000 decisions, ranging from trivial choices like what to eat for breakfast to life-altering ones such as changing careers or buying a house. Despite the central role that decision-making plays in human life, research in psychology and behavioural economics has consistently demonstrated that our choices are often far from rational. Understanding the cognitive biases and mental shortcuts that influence our decisions can help us make better choices and avoid common pitfalls.

One of the most well-documented phenomena in decision-making research is the anchoring effect, first described by psychologists Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman in the 1970s. The anchoring effect occurs when people rely too heavily on the first piece of information they encounter when making decisions. In a famous experiment, Tversky and Kahneman asked participants to spin a wheel of fortune that would land on either 10 or 65, and then estimate the percentage of African countries in the United Nations. Those who saw the number 65 estimated a significantly higher percentage than those who saw 10, despite the random number having no logical connection to the question. This demonstrates how even arbitrary numbers can serve as anchors that pull our judgments in their direction.

Another powerful bias is the status quo bias, which describes our tendency to prefer the current state of affairs even when change would be beneficial. This bias is closely related to loss aversion, a concept central to Kahneman and Tversky's Prospect Theory. Loss aversion refers to the finding that people experience losses roughly twice as intensely as equivalent gains. In other words, losing 100 pounds feels approximately twice as bad as gaining 100 pounds feels good. This asymmetry in how we process gains and losses has profound implications for everything from investment decisions to consumer behaviour.

The availability heuristic is a mental shortcut that leads people to judge the likelihood of events based on how easily examples come to mind. For instance, after seeing news reports about plane crashes, people tend to overestimate the danger of air travel, even though statistically it is far safer than driving. This heuristic explains why people often fear dramatic but rare risks — such as shark attacks or terrorist incidents — while underestimating more common but less sensational dangers, such as heart disease or road accidents.

Social psychologists have also identified the phenomenon of groupthink, which occurs when the desire for harmony within a group overrides a realistic appraisal of alternatives. The term was coined by psychologist Irving Janis in 1972 after analysing several high-profile policy failures, including the Bay of Pigs invasion. Groupthink tends to occur in cohesive groups with strong leaders, where members suppress dissenting opinions to maintain group unity. Historical examples range from the Challenger space shuttle disaster to the escalation of the Vietnam War.

More recently, researchers have explored the concept of choice overload, sometimes called the paradox of choice. Psychologist Sheena Iyengar demonstrated in a series of studies that while some choice is desirable, too many options can lead to decision fatigue, anxiety, and dissatisfaction. In one study, shoppers at a gourmet food store were offered samples of either 6 or 24 varieties of jam. While the larger display attracted more attention, shoppers were ten times more likely to actually purchase jam when presented with the smaller selection. This finding has significant implications for product design, marketing, and public policy, suggesting that simplifying choices can sometimes lead to better outcomes for consumers and citizens alike.

title.en: Passage 3 - Coral Reef Ecosystems Under Threat
title.zh: 文章3 - 受威胁的珊瑚礁生态系统

sections.passage:
Coral reefs are among the most biodiverse and economically valuable ecosystems on the planet. Often referred to as the 'rainforests of the sea', they occupy less than one percent of the ocean floor yet support approximately 25 percent of all marine species. Beyond their ecological significance, coral reefs provide critical services to human communities, including coastal protection from storms and erosion, food security for hundreds of millions of people, and livelihoods through tourism and fishing industries estimated to be worth over 375 billion dollars annually.

However, coral reefs worldwide are facing an unprecedented crisis. The primary threat is climate change, which affects corals through two main mechanisms. First, rising ocean temperatures cause coral bleaching, a phenomenon in which stressed corals expel the symbiotic algae called zooxanthellae that live within their tissues. These algae provide corals with up to 90 percent of their energy through photosynthesis and give them their vibrant colours. When zooxanthellae are expelled, the coral turns white and, if the stress persists, eventually dies. The longest global bleaching event on record occurred from 2014 to 2017, affecting reefs across every ocean and resulting in the death of approximately 30 percent of the corals on Australia's Great Barrier Reef.

The second mechanism through which climate change harms corals is ocean acidification. As the ocean absorbs increasing amounts of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, the water becomes more acidic, making it harder for corals and other calcifying organisms to build and maintain their calcium carbonate skeletons. Since the beginning of the Industrial Revolution, ocean pH has decreased by approximately 0.1 units, representing a roughly 26 percent increase in acidity. Scientists project that if current emission trends continue, ocean acidity could increase by a further 150 percent by 2100, potentially making it impossible for coral reefs to grow at all.

Beyond climate change, coral reefs face numerous local stressors that compound their vulnerability. Overfishing disrupts the ecological balance of reef ecosystems by removing key species that help maintain reef health. For example, parrotfish, which feed on algae that would otherwise smother corals, have been heavily overfished in many regions, leading to algal overgrowth that prevents coral recovery. Coastal development and agricultural runoff introduce sediment and pollutants that cloud the water and smother corals, while destructive fishing practices such as dynamite fishing and cyanide poisoning directly destroy reef structures.

Conservation efforts to protect and restore coral reefs are underway around the globe, employing a range of innovative strategies. Marine protected areas have been established in many reef regions, restricting fishing and other extractive activities to allow ecosystems to recover. Scientists are also pioneering coral gardening techniques, in which fragments of resilient coral species are grown in underwater nurseries before being transplanted onto degraded reefs. Perhaps most promisingly, researchers are using selective breeding and assisted evolution to develop coral strains that are more resistant to warmer temperatures and acidic conditions. In Hawaii, for example, scientists have identified 'super corals' that survived severe bleaching events and are studying their genetic traits to understand heat tolerance.

Despite these encouraging developments, most marine biologists agree that without significant reductions in greenhouse gas emissions, local conservation efforts alone will be insufficient to save the world's coral reefs. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change has warned that even a global temperature increase of 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels would result in the loss of 70 to 90 percent of coral reefs, while a 2-degree increase would destroy over 99 percent. The window of opportunity to preserve these vital ecosystems is rapidly closing, making the transition to renewable energy and sustainable practices not merely an environmental aspiration but an ecological imperative.
